body:
THREAT MODEL — assets, attackers, attacks, defenses, evidence

Assets/invariants: speaker notes/next preview/backstage messages remain presenter-only; only current controller changes authoritative public state; command ordering is deterministic; pairing grants expire and are single-use; session/account isolation; service availability. Trust boundaries: public display DOM/origin, private console origin, QR optical channel, browser-to-edge TLS, internal relay/broker, optional LAN peer path. Attackers: audience member with camera/QR visibility, malicious website in either browser, LAN peer, compromised display-origin JS/XSS/service worker, stolen/replayed URL/token, stale former controller, malicious tenant, network observer, overloaded client/server.

Attack -> defense -> verification evidence:
1. Audience photographs QR and races presenter. Defense: 256-bit fragment secret, <=120 s, atomic one-use redemption, authenticated account/deck authorization; for anonymous mode require display-local approval or compare a 4-word SAS on both devices. Short human codes alone need strict rate limiting; RFC 8628 section 5 covers brute force, remote phishing and session spying: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8628 . Test two simultaneous redeems: exactly one succeeds; unauthorized account cannot control deck.
2. Pair secret leaks through URL logs/referrer/history/analytics. Defense: fragment, immediate URL scrub, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, no third-party scripts on pair page, redact pairing/token fields from telemetry, CSP; secret hash/HMAC at rest. RFC 3986 says fragment is separated before dereference: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3986#section-3.5 . Test proxy/access logs contain pairingId but never secret.
3. Cross-site WebSocket hijacking/CSRF. Browser automatically attaches cookies. Defense: Secure HttpOnly SameSite=Strict host-only cookie; exact `Origin` allowlist during upgrade, Fetch Metadata where available, CSRF token for pairing mutation endpoints, reject `Origin:null`; authenticate and authorize every connection/message. RFC 6455 explicitly includes Origin for protection against unauthorized cross-origin use: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6455#section-10.2 . Test evil origin upgrade gets 403 despite valid cookie.
4. XSS/service worker on public display steals private state. Defense: separate `display.example.com` and `console.example.com`, no parent-domain cookie, distinct CSP/build/deploy/service workers; broker materializes role subscriptions and never serializes private payload to display. Origin boundary evidence RFC 6454: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6454 ; `__Host-` cookie draft: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis#section-4.1.3.2 . Canary test: seed unique secret note, capture every display HTTP/WS/RTC byte, assert canary absent; DISPLAY subscribe to private topic returns `TOPIC_FORBIDDEN`.
5. Client changes `role`, `sessionId`, topic, or tenant in JSON. Defense: derive auth tuple from socket session; typed inbound union; server constructs subscriptions; per-frame tenant/session/role/epoch ACL; no wildcard broker subjects. Fuzz test fields/topic names never expand privileges.
6. Replay/duplicate/out-of-order command changes slide twice. Defense: unique commandId idempotency table, baseRevision compare-and-set, monotonic revision, active controllerEpoch, absolute commands preferred. Test duplicate/reordered frames and reconnect replay yield one state transition.
7. Former/lost console keeps control after takeover. Defense: increment controllerEpoch transactionally, revoke prior lease/socket/session, reject all old frames, short session TTL and explicit end-presentation revoke. Test queued old command after takeover returns STALE_CONTROLLER.
8. WebRTC signaling MITM or peer substitution. DTLS encrypts channel but peer identity depends on authenticated fingerprint signaling; RFC 8827 explains fingerprints and signaling trust: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8827#section-4 . Defense: exchange offers/answers/ICE only over authenticated WSS within paired session; bind DTLS fingerprint to connection/role/epoch; do not authorize based on data-channel possession. Test modified fingerprint/signaling fails or produces a channel with no control authorization.
9. ICE candidate privacy and LAN exposure. Host/server-reflexive candidates reveal network information; TURN adds relay and credentials. Defense: optional WebRTC only after pairing/consent; `iceTransportPolicy:"relay"` for privacy-sensitive cloud mode or accept direct candidate exposure explicitly; ephemeral TURN credentials scoped to session/TTL; never expose private topics on RTC. RFC 8445: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8445 ; TURN authentication RFC 8656 section 3.2: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8656#section-3.2 .
10. UDP blocked or restrictive symmetric NAT makes P2P/WebTransport fail. Defense: WSS/TCP 443 remains canonical; WebRTC has TURN fallback but still needs operated relay; WebTransport must fall back because RFC 9114 says blocking UDP can prevent QUIC and clients should use TCP HTTP: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9114#section-3.1 . Chaos test blocks UDP and verifies control remains on WSS.
11. Oversized/high-rate frames or slow display causes memory/CPU exhaustion. Browser WebSocket API has no standardized inbound backpressure guarantee adequate for unbounded data; defense max 16 KiB control frames, schema depth/string bounds, per-role rates, bounded outbound queue, coalesce superseded public state, close 1009 for too large / 1008 policy violation, avoid sending slide assets over control channel. Load test slow consumer never grows queue without bound.
12. Notes leak via logs/errors/receipts/telemetry. Defense: explicit allowlisted DTO projection at producer (not redact later), separate sinks/access controls, never echo input on errors, data classification tests. Canary log scan and display-byte capture.
13. Broker/server operator sees private content. TLS/WSS is hop-to-server, not end-to-end against service. If operator-confidential notes are required, add application-layer E2EE with keys transferred via pairing and ciphertext-only broker; this complicates multi-console recovery/search. Do not imply WebRTC automatically solves it when signaling identity is server-controlled.
14. Downgrade to ws:// or insecure local relay. Defense: HTTPS/WSS only, HSTS, secure contexts, no automatic insecure LAN fallback. Fully offline mode requires provisioned trusted local certificate/relay.
15. Availability: QR guessing, connect storms, TURN exhaustion, reconnect herd. Defense: per-IP/account/pairing limits, quotas, full-jitter reconnect, bounded presence retention, ephemeral TURN credentials/bandwidth caps, observability alerts. Security controls must not put private payload values in metrics.

Attack/defense conclusion: separate origins are practical and worth the modest deployment cost, but are defense-in-depth; decisive confidentiality control is server-side role-specific serialization and broker ACL. The single strongest regression evidence is an end-to-end DISPLAY-role byte-capture canary proving a unique private note never crosses any display transport.

## EXPAND
- LEAD: Clarify whether cloud operator confidentiality/E2EE is a product requirement; it changes key recovery and multi-console design.
- LEAD: Clarify whether anonymous presenter pairing is allowed; without account authorization the display-local approval/SAS cannot be optional.
- DEAD END: Separate origins alone do not prevent backend/broker ACL mistakes or parent-domain cookie leakage; retain canary capture and host-only cookies.
summary: Attack-defense threat model with security tests
